sections.title: Welcome Session
paragraphs: Um but yeah, welcome everybody to the 2026 Protocol Symposium. This is day three, so you've actually probably been at the symposium already in the workshops um that happened in the last couple days, which were super fun. Um seems like it was busy times. The Discord was bumping in all the workshop channels. Um and I'm excited to get caught up on all the ones that I couldn't make it to. Um, as happens with these online events, it's like you kind of need the the time twister from Harry Potter to make it to everything. But fortunately for the talk tracks, it's primarily single track. So almost all the talks you'll be able to make it to. If you don't have other responsibilities outside of the symposium, um, if you are fully committed, you can probably attend like 97% of the talks, maybe 96. Um, and yeah, it should be good. So, thank you everybody for joining and sorry about the live streaming cancellation, but yeah, I heard rumors that Zoom got hacked by a a rogue swarm, so I'm just going to go with that. Um, yeah, I'd say I've got a few things to say here. And then, um, we've got David Lang, who's an alumni of the program, who many of you know, who's going to give a quick talk on field building. And then the next step is to get into a bit of a just open round table discussion between me, Tim, Benat, and David about field building, about protocol studies, about the symposium, about the protocol institute.

And then after that, we're going to go straight into the talk track in the 30-minute blocks. Um, so everybody will have a chance to, you know, comment, ask questions, engage in some friendly banter with with the speakers, and um, yeah. So, here we go.

First of all, um, stealing page from Simon's neck, starting with why, um, why are we here? And I think that one of the big reasons that those of you who have joined this opening session are here is that you're all researchers in some sort or students or, you know, you're building something and you need to take some, you know, indirect approaches to figuring out what's what the best step is. So yeah, the discord and protocol institute and the symposium in general is kind of a a way to get together and and have fun while doing that research, which you know can be kind of an individual activity, kind of quiet, kind of boring sometimes. There are stretches of research that are like quite tedious. So kind of giving everybody a good environment to do that research is really important and kind of something that we think about a lot. And then the symposium in particular is a chance once a year, once every other year for people working on protocol studies or protocol related things to come together, have a chance to connect, figure out some, you know, lighthouse ideas for guiding them the next year, some loose coordination.

Um and further to that, finding people that you want to work with and who can improve your work I think is another big aspect of the symposium. Like these this talk track is all about here's what I've been working on. Here's how it relates to protocol studies. I would really like some feedback on this. You'll get comments from people. Hopefully the SIG leads will give some feedback relative to their specific questions that they're working on. Um, and all in all, I think this is kind of working in the the spirit, not the letter of peer review. So, following that like idea that we should give each other feedback and like make sure that everybody's work is like up to a high standard. Not that there's any formal process for that right now obviously, but yeah, I think it's the spirit of peer review that's more important than the actual letter for or the stage that we're at. And lastly, um I think everybody is trying to make progress on something important to them. And then the symposium in general is a way for everybody to make progress on something important, which is protocol studies. And every year we should try and raise the bar a little bit and make sure that we're making progress on ideas, progress in how we do research, progress on um you know how we distribute these things, how education works for protocol studies generally. That I think is is a good goal for the symposium. You can think of it as like a ratcheting wrench where every time you turn it you should you should go a little further. should lock that progress in that you've made over the course of the year. So yeah, level up every time you come here, help other people do so.

And the theme for for this year is new nature. So I think this is um proven to be really compelling. Um it's a nice way to coordinate the various like research streams that are going on. um the folks that are doing research on memory versus stigm robotics um law. How do these things all fit into this idea that just like Alexander Humble invented nature a while ago as a concept like we have this kind of second generation of nature that we need to look at which isn't just the the biosphere and plant life and animal life but all the technology that's available as well which kind of seems to grow in these sort of evolutionary ways. And not only that has become just as much a part of the environment and affecting um like selection and mutation pressures that are affecting everything. So, it's a really great opportunity, I think, to adopt this frame and look at the world as kind of like um an explorer discover there's this that meme that goes around every once in a while where it's like you were born too late to explore the seas, too early to explore the stars, and just in time to do something blas and and normal. But you could take a more, you know, charitable approach and be like, you were born just in time to explore new nature, which is this, you know, technological um environment that's emerged in the last couple hundred years and is continuing to evolve very quickly. Um there are all sorts of interesting species of protocols and rules and technologies that like need to be studied. So yeah, it's time to go out and discover the laws of new nature. And I think that doing so with the lens of protocols is is very effective. There's a lot to be discovered. Um if you just AI for example is just a brand new field. There's stuff happening in medicine with protocols for um for how drugs are used to treat different diseases. um protocols, diplomacy obviously are increasingly important and it's not only just going out and discovering these things like I think that is the simple approach to this where you go out you discover new nature it's there for you to find it's there for you to document analyze and report back on but then there's al also this element that um you actually need to go out and invent new nature because half of it is technological and as we are, you know, creatures that can invent technology and improve technology and tinker with stuff. Um, yeah, like Spencer Normick says, born just in time for SAS. You can make new SAS as part of new nature. Um, but inventing is just as much a part of this process as discovery. So while you're going out and figuring out, oh, like look at these strange new laws of new nature, it's also an interesting lens beyond just biology in the sense that, you know, you can make inventions, you can improve the protocols that exist. You can take technologies and and make them better. You can figure out how to like replace something. And by doing so, you're affecting the laws. So, it's going to be a continually renewed process as well as like one that is not just observation but invention.

And one of the ways that I like to think about what's going on here is that everybody attending the symposium is a you know independent researcher. I don't think any of us are like very few of us are are formally associated with each other although there have been papers co-published by SOP alumni and and friends of so of now protocol institute um they're working together so new nature is kind of this this guiding thing that people are going to migrate towards and and explore and hopefully um protocol institute is the first swarmbased um research organization where all of these all of you brilliant researchers and people are going to like loosely work together and explore the space of of new nature very quickly and effectively outside of what would be a typical institution using the tools that are freshly available to you. making sure that everything is like in not only an innovation research but innovation methodology improving year after year and how we do these things.

So it's discovery and invention um inventing new methods discovering new laws inventing new laws discovering the effects of those things and it's going to be this ongoing process that hopefully is going to be a lot of fun and I'm really excited to see what everybody's come up with. um over the course of this past year. So with that said, I think it's worth just a a quick update on some, you know, context like what's happening with the protocol institute, where is that at? And um that being the the host of this protocol symposium this year, the first protocol symposium was of course hosted by summer protocols um two years ago as was the protocol school last year. And you can kind of think of this as like protocol institute is is base camp. So SOP is spinning out of the Ethereum Foundation officially. October 15th will be completely out of there. Protocol Institute will be out in the wild as this new base camp that all of you as adventurers, as explorers, as documenters of new nature can come back to for some respite to share what you found to connect with people and to plan new expeditions into the wild. So, the Discord is kind of home for that. We're hoping to continue to evolve it with with SIGs, with events, with support for people, the magazine, of course, the publishing, um, to kind of create a very strong, robust base camp out in the wild that people can use.

Um, yeah, and SIGs are special interest groups in case anybody missed the acronym. And further to that, we've been in this phase with summer protocols where we had a host with the Ethereum Foundation and it was this really great expansive um divergent process like for example in the first summer refusing to settle on one definition of protocols for the entire group having people come up with their own definitions. this is kind of um a highly divergent process that was an active choice to let that expand. Um you've we've also seen it in terms of the fields that we that have been brought in to the fellows have brought in for study for practice for improvement for education very very different the sigs operate autonomously we've had events artwork science fiction we've done lots and lots and lots of stuff um we've lots has been delegated to people to do as they see fit and it has been tremendously productive of um and part of the reason that that was possible is because of the um bandwidth afforded by the Ethereum Foundation.

And so we're in the we're in the hery phase of of this process where you decentralize till it hurts and recentralize till it works. Protocol Institute is kind of right now has a large scope and needs to come to some clear models of how to operate, what to focus on and new nature is a guiding philosophy is is that it's kind of a recentralization of the direction for research and on the side of the organization the SIGs the special interest groups are the way to recent iz till it works. So this is the kind of the engine of the protocol institute are the SIGs and we're like really going all in on having more SIGs, making sure they're working well, potentially up to 12 SIGs um is our ambitious topline um goal for how many that we could sustain at at a high quality at good tempo. And the goal is that the SIGs would advance their own research themes and work together to synthesize findings um as a part of the protocol institute. So you can kind of think of this like an engine. The more sigs that we have, the faster and stronger we're going to be able to go, the more quickly we're going to be able to synthesize the laws of new nature.
And this is how we're going to create more impact down the road. My hope is that um we're starting with a V6 engine.

Hopefully we can get up to a V12 engine. And this is going to like have a big impact on popular science, people's worldviews. We've already seen um protocol studies enter educational curriculums around the world, which is awesome. And by having that broader impact and appeal and seeing this appear in the wild is going to generate the ability to bring in funding or the protocol institute which can be directed into existing SIGs to level up into new SIGs to expand or deepen areas of research into processes of synthesis into new projects that are like more capital intensive, more interesting And yeah, like Benat said, the fun part of this flywheel is is under construction. The sigs, we have a good model for that and can, you know, go from V6 to V12, you know, pretty sensibly, but yeah, this is an ongoing process and it's the early days.

One of the downsides of using an engine as an analogy is that it seems very straightforward. It's concurrent. Um you can just fit in the puzzle pieces that you don't have. But another way to look at um proto protocol institute and this process of um recentralization is as protocol studies and as researchers as like a frontier species of lychen. So the way that lykan forms is when hot magma comes up onto the earth and hardens it contains a lot of trace minerals and stuff like that but it's very harsh not much can can live on it. So one way to think of the SIGs also are as these different pieces of lychen that are populating a hot bed of magma which is the corpus of protocol studies so far and the effects it's had um however small elsewhere. So in the early days this is going to be a very like quickly evolving like difficult process that is going to look different from year to year month to month or even week to week um depending on what's going on. So on the one hand you've got this engine and the flywheel that you're trying to build.

parts of it are in construction like the fund and and how to establish that like how to get the marketing right for the impact of protocol studies versus the value that people are willing to invest in it. On the other hand, you've got this like much more organic view which is that there are a bunch of research streams going on. Some of them are going to take off really well. Some of them aren't going to do as well. There are going to be people coming in and out. there are going to be new projects and old projects and projects that get revived that you thought were like completely done but they've they've come back for a second win. So keep this in mind too. It's not just a straightforward engineering process building this thing. Um it is very much like the people who are involved that make this thing great. So continuing to be involved is one of the best things you can do whether or not you're a part of a SIG, whether or not you're leading a SIG, whether or not you're part of building that flywheel, continuing to contribute in some way is is important because you're part of the ecology of of Protocol Institute in a sense.

So just light housekeeping notes. I'll go into more detail later. Keep the schedule handy. Um it's just on the protocol institute.org/symposium page. You'll get a Zoom link each morning. Ping me on Discord if you have questions or anything or in the Zoom chat. Um I've put the slides on the YouTube. Um I'll share them here in the Zoom chat as well. Um and almost everything is recorded or live streamed. Um live stream TBD. We'll see if I can um fix that. Everything's being recorded. Unless you don't want to be recorded, just ping me. Um, if you are running a session that you don't want to be recorded, that's okay. We'll make it work. Um, if you don't want to be recorded as a person, just turn your camera off and and um send messages in the chat. You can change your name to something like like Octopus 7 or like cow and UFO. Um,
